Chapter Two — How This Book Grows: A Protocol for Future Additions
Cannabis is the proof of concept. It does not have to be the last addition — and it does not have to be the compiler’s own hand that makes the next one.
No second plant is currently under review. What follows instead is an open invitation, addressed to no one in particular and everyone who qualifies: any future Architect — a researcher, a clinician, a student, a collaborator this book has not met yet — may propose the next addition, on the condition that it is built the way this one was. The invitation is the point, not a placeholder for a plant already chosen. A name offered before the method has been followed would be exactly the mistake this book exists to avoid.
For any future Architect — collaborator, editor, or a later version of the person who compiled this book — considering whether a new plant, compound, or system belongs in Earth’s Pharmacy, the standard is the same one applied here:
1. History first. Establish where the plant or practice actually comes from — which traditions used it, how, and for how long. Distinguish documented history from inference, and inference from speculation.
2. Mechanism second. Describe how the plant or compound interacts with human physiology, where that is known. Mechanism is background, not verdict.
3. Evidence, tiered honestly. Apply the four-tier grid to each specific claim — not to the plant as a whole. A plant can hold a Tier 1 claim and a Tier 4 claim at the same time, for two different uses.
4. Harm given equal billing with benefit. Every caution, interaction, and population-specific risk gets stated as plainly as every benefit. A chapter that only lists benefits has not met this book’s standard, regardless of how well-cited it is.
5. Law kept separate from science. Legal status, scheduling, and regulatory change are recorded as facts with a date attached. They are never treated as evidence of safety, efficacy, or the reverse.
6. Built to be revised. Every claim, tier, and legal note in this book is written to be corrected by better evidence, not defended against it. Date every regulatory claim. Flag every section that will age quickly. Assume a future Architect will need to update this page, and make that update easy rather than adversarial.
7. No special doors. The same standard applies whether the subject is fashionable, controversial, profitable, illegal, or beloved. A plant does not get a lighter evidentiary standard because it is popular, and it does not get a harsher one because it is unpopular.
Any future contributor — including readers, researchers, or collaborators who wish to propose a plant for inclusion — can use this seven-point protocol as a submission standard. A proposed chapter that follows it can be evaluated on its merits. One that does not will be sent back to follow it, regardless of who submitted it or how compelling the plant’s story is.
The architecture provides continuity. Evidence provides direction. Growth is part of the design.
GLOSSARY OF HEALING TERMS ACROSS TRADITIONS
Alkaline/electric food — Dr. Sebi’s term for foods he taught were life-giving and non-mucus-forming; a belief-system term used descriptively in the Ode, not adopted as this book’s medical framework.
Bissap — West African (especially Senegalese) name for hibiscus tea; called sorrel in the Caribbean.
Bush medicine — the everyday, home- and community-based herbal healing tradition of the Caribbean, distinct from formalized clinical medicine.
Cerasee — Caribbean name for bitter melon vine, brewed as a traditional bitter tonic tea.
Decoction — a preparation made by simmering roots, bark, or tough plant material in water, as opposed to simply steeping.
Efirin — Yoruba name for African basil (Ocimum gratissimum).
Fever grass — Caribbean name for lemongrass, traditionally brewed for fevers and colds.
Infusion — a preparation made by steeping leaves or flowers in hot water; what most people mean by “tea.”
Mucus theory — Dr. Sebi’s belief that disease originates from mucus accumulation in the body; presented in this book as his teaching, not as established medical fact.
Root doctor — a traditional Black American herbalist and healer, especially in the Southern folk-medicine tradition.
Tier system — this book’s own honesty framework (Tier 1: research-supported; Tier 2: promising; Tier 3: traditional use only) used to rate every claim about every plant.
Washout — Caribbean term for a traditional cleansing or purging remedy, often using bitter herbs.

BIBLIOGRAPHY
This section will grow batch by batch as claims are verified against real sources, mirroring the structure of the plant monographs themselves. No claim is added here from memory — only from a confirmed search. Any claim that fails to find real support during this process is downgraded honestly in its monograph rather than left uncited.
Citation Batch 1 — COMPLETE (Monographs 1–5):
Ginger — nausea and vomiting in pregnancy (Monograph #1, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED): Viljoen, E., Visser, J., Koen, N., & Musekiwa, A. (2014). “A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect and safety of ginger in the treatment of pregnancy-associated nausea and vomiting.” Nutrition Journal, 13(20). DOI: 10.1186/1475-2891-13-20. Twelve RCTs, 1,278 pregnant women; ginger significantly improved nausea versus placebo with no safety concerns identified.
Turmeric/curcumin — osteoarthritis joint pain (Monograph #2, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED): Wang, Z., Singh, A., Jones, G., Winzenberg, T., Ding, C., Chopra, A., et al. (2021). “Efficacy and safety of turmeric extracts for the treatment of knee osteoarthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.” Current Rheumatology Reports, 23(11). DOI: 10.1007/s11926-020-00975-8. Multiple meta-analyses (up to 15 RCTs, 1,621+ participants across pooled reviews) show real reductions in pain and stiffness scores versus placebo; bioavailability remains a genuine limiting factor, consistent with this book’s original tier placement.
Garlic — blood pressure (Monograph #3, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED): Ried, K., Frank, O.R., Stocks, N.P., Fakler, P., & Sullivan, T. (2008). “Effect of garlic on blood pressure: a systematic review and meta-analysis.” BMC Cardiovascular Disorders, 8(13). Meta-analysis found a mean systolic blood pressure reduction of 4.6 mmHg overall, and 8.4 mmHg in the hypertensive subgroup specifically, versus placebo.
Hibiscus — blood pressure (Monograph #4, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, with an honest nuance): Serban, C., Sahebkar, A., Ursoniu, S., Andrica, F., & Banach, M. (2015). “Effect of sour tea (Hibiscus sabdariffa L.) on arterial hypertension: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.” Journal of Hypertension, 33(6), 1119–1127. DOI: 10.1097/HJH.0000000000000585. Confirms a real, modest blood-pressure-lowering effect; one earlier systematic review found the evidence “not fully conclusive” for primary hypertension specifically, which is why this book’s original wording (“modest but real”) stands rather than overstating the effect.
Moringa — blood sugar support (Monograph #5, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED): Systematic review and meta-analysis, “Moringa oleifera on hyperglycemia and hypertension in metabolic diseases: Systematic review, exploratory meta-analysis and meta-regression” (2025/2026), Clinical Nutrition Open Science (ScienceDirect). Twenty human clinical studies in patients with metabolic disease found a modest association between moringa supplementation and reduced fasting blood glucose (SMD −0.70) and HbA1c (MD −0.62%) — consistent with this book’s original “Promising” tier rather than a stronger claim.
Aloe vera — burns and wound healing (Monograph #6, Tier 1/2 — CONFIRMED): Huang, Y.N., Chen, K.C., Wang, J.H., & Lin, Y.K. (2024). “Effects of Aloe vera on Burn Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.” Journal of Burn Care & Research, 45(6), 1536–1545. DOI: 10.1093/jbcr/irae061. Nine RCTs; aloe vera reduced wound-healing time by a mean of 3.76 days versus other topical treatments, without increased infection risk.
Bitter melon (cerasee) — blood sugar (Monograph #9, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED, genuinely mixed): Multiple systematic reviews return contradictory results. Fuangchan, A., et al. (2011). “Hypoglycemic effect of bitter melon compared with metformin in newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes patients.” Journal of Ethnopharmacology, 134(2), 422–428. A separate 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis (PMC10808600) concluded the metabolic effect “cannot be determined based on the available clinical evidence” — confirming this book’s original framing of real biological activity without established treatment-level evidence.
Elderberry — cold and flu symptom duration (Monograph #15, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED): Hawkins, J., Baker, C., Cherry, L., & Dunne, E. (2019). “Black elderberry (Sambucus nigra) supplementation effectively treats upper respiratory symptoms: a meta-analysis of randomized, controlled clinical trials.” Complementary Therapies in Medicine, 42, 361–365. Meta-analysis of 4 RCTs found elderberry reduced upper respiratory symptom duration and severity, including flu recovery roughly 4 days sooner than placebo.
Nettle — allergic rhinitis (Monograph #14, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, modest): Mittman, P. (1990). “Randomized, double-blind study of freeze-dried Urtica dioica in the treatment of allergic rhinitis.” Planta Medica, 56(1), 44–47. PMID: 2192379. The foundational trial: 58% of the nettle group rated it moderately-to-highly effective versus 37% on placebo — a real but modest effect, consistent with this book’s original wording.
Dandelion — mild diuretic effect (Monograph #11, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED): Clare, B.A., Conroy, R.S., & Spelman, K. (2009). “The diuretic effect in human subjects of an extract of Taraxacum officinale folium over a single day.” Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine, 15(8), 929–934. DOI: 10.1089/acm.2008.0152. Small pilot study (n=17); significant increase in urination frequency confirmed in humans for the first time, though the authors themselves call for further study — consistent with this book’s “Promising,” not overstated, tier placement.
Soursop leaf/seed — annonacin neurotoxicity caution (Monograph #8, and Monograph #81 custard apple — CONFIRMED AND STRENGTHENED): Lannuzel, A., Michel, P.P., Caparros-Lefebvre, D., Abaul, J., Hocquemiller, R. (2002). “Toxicity of Annonaceae for dopaminergic neurons: potential role in atypical parkinsonism in Guadeloupe.” Movement Disorders, 17(1), 84–90. Champy, P., et al. (2005). “Quantification of acetogenins in Annona muricata linked to atypical parkinsonism in Guadeloupe.” Movement Disorders, 20(12), 1629–1633. Real, well-documented epidemiological and toxicological evidence: in Guadeloupe, roughly two-thirds of all parkinsonism cases are the atypical form linked to heavy Annonaceae consumption, versus under 30% in Europe. This caution was correctly placed in the original draft and the underlying science is, if anything, more serious than originally stated.
Sea moss — iodine content and thyroid caution (Monograph #10 — CONFIRMED): Teas, J., et al. (2004) established Chondrus crispus iodine content averaging approximately 3.8 µg/g dry weight, though batch variation is significant; a 45-gram serving can provide roughly 2.1 mg of iodine, nearly double the adult tolerable upper intake level of 1,100 µg/day. Leung, A.M., & Braverman, L.E. (2014). “Consequences of excess iodine.” Nature Reviews Endocrinology, 10(3), 136–142. Confirms both the Wolff-Chaikoff (hypothyroid) and Jod-Basedow (hyperthyroid) mechanisms by which excess iodine genuinely disrupts thyroid function — this book’s caution was correctly placed and, if anything, understates how easily an ordinary serving can exceed safe iodine limits.
Kola nut — stimulant effect (Monograph #17, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED): Well-established pharmacological fact across multiple food-science and clinical references (Cleveland Clinic; Drugs.com natural products monograph; Burdock, G. [2009], safety assessment published in Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology): kola nut contains approximately 2–3.5% caffeine by dry weight, and a single nut can contain more caffeine than two large cups of coffee. This is straightforward, non-controversial pharmacology, consistent with the original Tier 1 designation.
Peppermint (oil) — irritable bowel syndrome (Monograph #22, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED): Alammar, N., et al. (2019). “The impact of peppermint oil on the irritable bowel syndrome: a meta-analysis of the pooled clinical data.” BMC Complementary Medicine and Therapies, 19(21). Twelve RCTs, 835 patients; enteric-coated peppermint oil significantly outperformed placebo for global IBS symptoms and abdominal pain. One large 2019 trial found mixed results on its primary endpoint while still showing benefit on secondary measures — a genuine nuance consistent with this book’s original tier placement.
Chamomile — anxiety and sleep (Monograph #21, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, with honest nuance): Hieu, T.H., et al. (2019). “Therapeutic efficacy and safety of chamomile for state anxiety, generalized anxiety disorder, insomnia, and sleep quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials and quasi-randomized trials.” Phytotherapy Research, 33(6), 1604–1615. Twelve RCTs found a significant, real effect on generalized anxiety disorder specifically; evidence for simple situational (“state”) anxiety and for insomnia specifically was weaker and more mixed. This book’s original wording (“mild anxiety and modestly improved sleep quality”) holds up reasonably, though the anxiety evidence is stronger than the sleep-specific evidence.
Cascara sagrada — laxative effect (Monograph #28, Tier 1 → DOWNGRADED to Tier 2): This is the first genuine correction the citation process has found. U.S. Food and Drug Administration (2002) ruled that nonprescription cascara sagrada laxative products were no longer “generally recognized as safe and effective,” citing insufficient evidence. Müller-Lissner, S. (2010) systematic review found no clinically important results from randomized controlled trials for cascara in adults with chronic idiopathic constipation. The stimulant mechanism (via cascarosides and emodin) is real and pharmacologically understood, but this book’s original Tier 1 claim overstated the modern clinical trial support. The monograph has been corrected accordingly — this is exactly the kind of catch this process exists to make.
Devil’s claw — osteoarthritis and joint pain (Monograph #33, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, with honest nuance on study quality): Brien, S., Lewith, G.T., & McGregor, G. (2006). “Devil’s Claw (Harpagophytum procumbens) as a treatment for osteoarthritis: a review of efficacy and safety.” Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine, 12(10), 981–993. Fourteen clinical trials reviewed; higher-quality studies showed real effectiveness for reducing pain, though the reviewers themselves noted meaningful methodological weaknesses across many of the included trials and called for more definitive research. This book’s Tier 1 placement holds as one of the better-evidenced African botanicals for joint pain specifically, with the appropriate caveat that trial quality varies.
Willow bark — mild-to-moderate pain (Monograph #99, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, strongest for low back pain specifically): Chrubasik, S., et al. (2000). “Treatment of low back pain exacerbations with willow bark extract: a randomized double-blind study.” American Journal of Medicine, 109(1), 9–14. A 2014 Cochrane review of 2 trials (261 participants) found moderate-quality evidence favoring willow bark over placebo for short-term low back pain relief. Evidence for osteoarthritis specifically is real but more modest (Schmid et al., 2001, Phytotherapy Research: statistically significant but small effect size). One 2019 U.S. military-oriented review recommended against relying on it for general chronic musculoskeletal pain. This book’s Tier 1 placement is best supported for low back pain specifically, with osteoarthritis benefit being real but smaller than the general framing suggested.
Feverfew — migraine prevention (Monograph #100, Tier 1 → DOWNGRADED to Tier 2): Second genuine correction. Cochrane systematic review (Wider, B., et al., 2015, updated) found trial results too heterogeneous to pool reliably; the largest, most rigorous trial (n=218) showed a real but modest benefit (~0.6 fewer migraine attacks per month than placebo). A 2025 meta-analysis of 3 trials (naturalmedfacts.com) found a non-significant reduction in frequency, while a separate 2025 review of 9 trials found a significant frequency reduction but no effect on severity. The effect is real and biologically plausible but genuinely inconsistent across the highest-quality reviews — corrected from Tier 1 to Tier 2 accordingly.
Ashwagandha — stress and cortisol (Monograph #96, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, strong): Systematic review and meta-analysis (2024), Journal of Ethnopharmacology or equivalent (PMID: 39348746): nine RCTs, 558 patients. Ashwagandha significantly reduced Perceived Stress Scale scores (MD = −4.72), Hamilton Anxiety Scale scores (MD = −2.19), and serum cortisol (MD = −2.58) compared to placebo. A more recent 2026 dose-response meta-analysis confirms the effect while noting genuine heterogeneity across studies and calling for more high-certainty trials — a normal caveat that does not undercut the real, repeatedly-replicated core finding. One of the more robustly confirmed Tier 1 claims in this book.
Licorice root — reflux/DGL and the blood pressure caution (Monograph #95, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED, caution strongly validated): The mechanism is well-established pharmacology: glycyrrhizin inhibits the enzyme 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2, causing sodium retention, potassium loss, and elevated blood pressure (a condition termed pseudohyperaldosteronism) — confirming this book’s caution precisely. Deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) removes most glycyrrhizin and shows real, if modest, clinical benefit for functional dyspepsia (e.g., the GutGard 150mg/day trial) without the cardiovascular risk. This book’s original Tier 2 placement and whole-licorice-vs-DGL distinction is fully confirmed by the literature.
Valerian root — sleep (Monograph #97, Tier 1 → DOWNGRADED to Tier 2): Third genuine correction. Bent, S., et al. (2006). “Valerian for Sleep: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.” American Journal of Medicine, 119(12), 1005–1012. Sixteen RCTs, 1,093 patients; found significant benefit on a dichotomous “improved/not improved” measure but flagged clear evidence of publication bias in that result. Subsequent reviews using objective sleep measures (actigraphy, polysomnography) have generally not shown benefit over placebo, with one DARE-indexed review concluding evidence did not support valerian’s clinical efficacy for insomnia. Corrected from Tier 1 to Tier 2.
Lavender — anxiety, via oral Silexan preparation (Monograph #93, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, strong): Kasper, S., et al. (2014). “Lavender oil preparation Silexan is effective in generalized anxiety disorder — a randomized, double-blind comparison to placebo and paroxetine.” International Journal of Neuropsychopharmacology, 17(6), 859–869. In a 539-patient trial, oral lavender oil (Silexan, 80–160mg/day) performed comparably to paroxetine, an established prescription SSRI, and significantly outperformed placebo. Licensed as a medicinal product in 14 countries. A 2019 meta-analysis of subthreshold anxiety trials and a 2019 network meta-analysis both confirm the effect. This is one of the more rigorously confirmed Tier 1 claims in the entire book — the standardized oral capsule form specifically, not casual tea.
Passionflower — anxiety (Monograph #98, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, small-trial caveat): Akhondzadeh, S., et al. (2001). “Passionflower in the treatment of generalized anxiety: a pilot double-blind randomized controlled trial with oxazepam.” Journal of Clinical Pharmacy and Therapeutics, 26(5), 363–367. Thirty-six patients; passionflower extract performed comparably to oxazepam (a prescription benzodiazepine) for generalized anxiety disorder. A 2020 systematic review of nine clinical trials found the majority showed reduced anxiety, with less clear benefit specifically in people with only mild anxiety. This book’s Tier 1 placement holds, with the honest caveat that supporting trials are generally small-scale pilot studies rather than large confirmatory trials.
Rooibos — antioxidant activity (Monograph #29, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED): Marnewick, J.L., et al. (2011). “Effects of Rooibos (Aspalathus linearis) on Oxidative Stress and Biochemical Parameters in Adults at Risk for Cardiovascular Disease.” Journal of Ethnopharmacology, 133(1), 46–52. Six weeks of daily fermented rooibos consumption significantly improved lipid profile and redox status (oxidative stress markers) in adults at cardiovascular risk — a genuinely well-conducted human trial, one of the few in this book’s antioxidant-tea category with real clinical (not just laboratory) evidence. Confirms this book’s Tier 2 placement.
Fenugreek — blood sugar (Monograph #59, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, strong): Systematic review and meta-analysis (2023), International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Ten RCTs, 706 participants; fenugreek significantly reduced fasting blood glucose, 2-hour postprandial glucose, and HbA1c versus control, with no hepatic or renal toxicity observed. A separate 2024 meta-analysis confirmed similar significant reductions. One of the more robustly confirmed Tier 1 claims in this book.
Milk thistle (silymarin) — liver support (Monograph #77, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, strongest for drug-induced injury and NAFLD): Tao, L., et al. (2019). “Prophylactic Therapy of Silymarin (Milk Thistle) on Antituberculosis Drug-Induced Liver Injury: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.” Canadian Journal of Gastroenterology and Hepatology. Five RCTs, 1,198 patients; silymarin significantly reduced liver injury incidence and protected liver enzyme levels. Separately, a 26-RCT, 2,375-patient meta-analysis found benefit for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Evidence for hepatitis C specifically was notably weaker (a 2014 meta-analysis found no significant difference from placebo on viral load or liver enzymes) — this book’s Tier 1 claim holds best for drug-induced liver injury and NAFLD, less so for viral hepatitis specifically.
Pygeum (African cherry) — benign prostatic hyperplasia (Monograph #118, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, modest effect): Ishani, A., et al. (2000). “Pygeum africanum for the treatment of patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia: a systematic review and quantitative meta-analysis.” American Journal of Medicine, 109(8), 654–664. Eighteen RCTs, 1,562 men; pygeum “modestly, but significantly” improved urologic symptoms and flow measures. A genuine African-bark-to-global-medicine story, though the reviewers note the effect size is modest, not dramatic, consistent with this book’s honest framing.
Cacao — heart and vascular health (Monograph #52, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED): Hooper, L., et al. (2012). “Effects of chocolate, cocoa, and flavan-3-ols on cardiovascular health: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials.” American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. A separate DARE-indexed meta-analysis (10 RCTs, 297 individuals) confirmed flavanol-rich cocoa products significantly reduce blood pressure and improve vascular/endothelial function. Confirms this book’s Tier 1 designation for minimally processed, high-flavanol cacao specifically — not ordinary sugared chocolate.
Echinacea — cold prevention/duration (Monograph #58, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED, genuinely mixed exactly as written): Karsch-Völk, M., et al. (2014). “Echinacea for preventing and treating the common cold.” Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. Twenty-four trials, 4,631 participants; found a modest, borderline-significant prevention effect (10% absolute risk reduction, number needed to treat = 10) but limited effect on cold duration once symptomatic. A separate 2007 meta-analysis (Shah et al., Lancet Infectious Diseases) found a stronger effect (58% reduced odds of catching a cold, 1.4 fewer sick days). The genuine inconsistency across reviews confirms this book’s original “honestly inconsistent” framing precisely — no correction needed.
Comfrey — pyrrolizidine alkaloid liver toxicity caution (Monograph #74 — CONFIRMED, strongly): LiverTox (NIH/NCBI, updated 2022) and multiple peer-reviewed reviews (Stedman, 2002, Seminars in Liver Disease; Roitman, 1981, The Lancet) confirm comfrey’s pyrrolizidine alkaloids cause hepatic sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (veno-occlusive disease), with infants especially vulnerable. Internal use is restricted or banned in most countries for exactly this reason. This book’s hard “no internal use” caution is fully and precisely confirmed by the literature — no softening warranted.
African potato — HIV/antiretroviral interaction caution (Monograph #65 — CONFIRMED, with honest refinement): Real interaction mechanisms confirmed: African potato affects CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein drug-metabolizing pathways relevant to antiretroviral drugs (cited in a 2015 clinically-relevant herb-drug interaction review), and an animal study found combined use with antiretroviral therapy worsened liver histopathology markers. One small human study of acute, short-term hypoxoside exposure in HIV patients found no significant hepatic/renal test changes — but this was acute-dosing only, not long-term combined use. This book’s caution about combining African potato with HIV treatment is well-founded; the honest refinement is that direct human hepatotoxicity data is more limited than the animal/mechanistic data, though the interaction risk itself is real and documented.
Cassia (wild senna) — laxative effect (Monograph #39, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, genuinely holds up better than cascara): Unlike cascara sagrada, senna remains actively recommended by the American Gastroenterological Association/American College of Gastroenterology (conditional recommendation) for chronic idiopathic constipation, based on real randomized controlled trial evidence, and has not been withdrawn from FDA recognition. This book’s original Tier 1, short-term-use-only framing is accurate and, notably, holds up better under scrutiny than the parallel cascara sagrada claim did — a useful contrast confirming the citation process catches both false positives and true positives correctly.
Cat’s claw — joint pain/rheumatoid arthritis (Monograph #26, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED): Mur, E., Hartig, F., Eibl, G., & Schirmer, M. (2002). “Randomized double-blind trial of an extract from the pentacyclic alkaloid-chemotype of Uncaria tomentosa for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis.” Journal of Rheumatology, 29(4), 678–681. Forty patients; cat’s claw reduced painful joint count versus placebo as an adjuvant to standard RA treatment, well tolerated with no liver injury (confirmed separately by NIH LiverTox). Piscoya, J., et al. (2001) found improved subjective pain scores in 45 knee osteoarthritis patients, though objective swelling measures did not change. Small trial sizes throughout — this book’s “several small human trials, larger confirmatory trials still needed” framing is accurate.
Sutherlandia (cancer bush) — the name correction (Monograph #122 — CONFIRMED, strongly, with an additional real caution found): A 2025 systematic review (Planta Medica/related, “An Example of Promotional Research, or Is There Scientific Merit?”) concluded that S. frutescens “does not exhibit acceptable levels of bioactivity/selectivity” for cancer treatment and “should not currently be recommended for use” given cancer’s seriousness — precisely confirming this book’s direct correction of the plant’s misleading common name. An additional real finding: in a safety trial of HIV-positive adults, two participants developed tuberculosis despite taking isoniazid (TB-preventive medication) while also taking Sutherlandia, suggesting a possible interaction that reduces isoniazid’s protective effect — a genuine interaction caution this book’s monograph should note alongside its existing HIV-medication caution. Separately, general safety trials in healthy adults found no significant adverse effects at studied doses.
Boneset — fever/flu support (Monograph #133, Tier 3 — CONFIRMED, caution STRENGTHENED with a real correction): Colegate, S.M., et al. (2018). “Potentially toxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids in Eupatorium perfoliatum and three related species. Implications for herbal use as boneset.” Phytochemical Analysis, 29(6), 613–626. Direct chemical analysis (HPLC-MS) of 49 boneset samples confirmed dehydropyrrolizidine alkaloids are present in the species itself — not merely in related plants, as the original draft stated — across dried leaf, tinctures, and hot-water preparations alike. The researchers explicitly call for “preclusive caution.” The monograph’s caution text has been corrected to reflect this direct (not merely related-species) finding.
Wormwood, African variant — respiratory/digestive support (Monograph #40, Tier 2/3 — CONFIRMED): This monograph correctly distinguishes Artemisia afra (the milder African species discussed) from Artemisia absinthium (the higher-thujone European species used in absinthe). Real search confirms this distinction matters: A. absinthium carries genuine thujone-toxicity concerns at high doses or with prolonged use (European Medicines Agency guidance limits use), while African wormwood is traditionally regarded as milder — exactly as the monograph states. No changes needed.
Bladderwrack — iodine/thyroid nutrition (Monograph #20, Tier 2 with strong caution — CONFIRMED): WebMD/Drugs.com clinical compilation and case reports (e.g., a lithium patient who developed hyperthyroidism after taking Fucus vesiculosus as a laxative) confirm bladderwrack’s iodine content is highly variable (documented up to 600–8,000 mcg per 100g) and can cause thyroid dysfunction in both directions, plus documented heavy-metal/arsenic contamination risk depending on harvest location. This monograph’s framing as “one of the most important caution flags in the book” is fully justified by the evidence. No changes needed.
Uva ursi (bearberry) — urinary tract support (Monograph #76, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED): Multiple sources (European Medicines Agency guidance, LiverTox, Christopher Hobbs clinical database) confirm short-term-only use (1–2 weeks maximum) is the correct standard due to hydroquinone-related liver/kidney concern with prolonged use, though a 2013 risk-assessment study (Garcia de Arriba et al., Human & Experimental Toxicology) found actual risk at recommended short-term doses is lower than older fears suggested. This monograph’s caution framing holds up accurately. No changes needed.
Noni — general wellness marketing claims (Monograph #82, Tier 2/unproven with strong caution — CONFIRMED): Real, published case reports confirm noni juice-associated liver injury, including Millonig et al. (2005, World Journal of Gastroenterology) reporting two cases of hepatotoxicity — one requiring liver transplantation after 1.5L consumed over 3 weeks — plus additional case reports in a 14-year-old boy and a woman on concurrent anticonvulsant therapy. This monograph’s liver-injury caution and skepticism toward sweeping marketing claims is fully justified and, if anything, understated relative to how serious some documented cases have been. No changes needed, though the caution’s severity is well-earned.
Cat’s claw — joint pain (see entry #26 above, already logged).
Neem — skin/antimicrobial/dental use (Monograph #16, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED): Drugs.com clinical compilation confirms reasonable antimicrobial evidence exists (mostly lab/animal-level for internal uses like malaria, stronger for topical/dental applications), and explicitly confirms this book’s strongest caution: oral neem oil in children has been linked to reported deaths, so internal use is not supported. This monograph’s framing — Tier 2 for topical/dental, hard “not for internal use, especially in children” caution — is fully accurate. No changes needed.
Jamaican dogwood — sedative/pain use (Monograph #84, Tier 3 with serious caution — CONFIRMED): Multiple clinical references (WebMD, ADAM/Lima Memorial, Restorative Medicine monograph) confirm real pharmacological activity (rotenoid/isoflavonoid content acting on mitochondrial complex I, comparable in animal studies to valerian/passionflower-range sedation) alongside genuine toxicity concern at excess doses and a documented anesthesia-interaction caution. This monograph’s “not a casual home tea, qualified herbalist only” framing matches the clinical literature closely. No changes needed.
Pumpkin seed — antiparasitic use (Monograph #67, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED): A 2019 human clinical study (Alhawiti et al., Acta Parasitologica) found pumpkin seed extract combined with areca nut extract achieved 89% efficacy against tapeworm (Hymenolepis nana) in humans; multiple additional animal studies confirm activity against roundworms and other intestinal nematodes via the compound cucurbitin. This is real human data, though limited to one primary trial — this book’s “real laboratory evidence… modern human clinical confirmation is limited” framing is accurate and appropriately calibrated. No changes needed.
Sarsaparilla — anti-inflammatory/skin &** joint use (Monograph #13, Tier 2/3 — CONFIRMED, well-calibrated):** Real search found a mixed picture worth noting: some older/popular herbal sources cite a 1942 uncontrolled 92-patient study claiming strong psoriasis improvement, but rigorous modern review (Drugs.com clinical compilation, 2025) states direct clinical evidence for psoriasis specifically is lacking and no modern controlled human trials exist. This book did NOT overclaim the old psoriasis study — it correctly limits itself to “anti-inflammatory & skin (Tier 2 — Promising)… direct human clinical trials remain limited” and keeps joint-comfort at Tier 3 traditional use. This is exactly right calibration. No changes needed.
Corn silk — mild diuretic effect (Monograph #57, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED): Real search found genuinely mixed evidence matching this book’s “reasonable traditional and preliminary scientific support” framing: multiple animal studies (Maksimovic et al. 2004, Pharmazie) confirm real diuretic activity, but the one located human trial (38 volunteers, one week) found no significant difference from control, likely due to low dose. This book’s modest, hedged Tier 2 framing (not Tier 1) is the accurate call given this mixed human/animal picture. No changes needed.
Amla (Indian gooseberry) — blood sugar &** cholesterol support (Monograph #137, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED):** A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicenter trial (98 dyslipidemic patients, published in BMC Complementary and Alternative Medicine) found amla extract significantly reduced total cholesterol, LDL, and triglycerides versus placebo over 12 weeks, and additional trials/meta-analyses confirm similar effects on fasting glucose and CRP. This is genuinely solid human trial evidence — arguably even stronger than this book’s conservative “some encouraging human trial evidence for modest supportive effects” framing suggests, though the conservative framing is not inaccurate. Vitamin C content claim independently confirmed as exceptionally high (193–720 mg/100g across cultivars). No changes needed.
Guinea hen weed (anamu) — anti-inflammatory/pain, “cancer herb” reputation (Monograph #25 — CONFIRMED, with a real caution added): This monograph was already exceptionally well-calibrated — correctly flagging the popular “cancer herb” reputation as unsupported by human trials (matching Drugs.com’s explicit “clinical data are lacking to support use for any therapeutic use,” 2025). Real search surfaced one additional documented finding not in the original caution: the plant contains low concentrations of coumadin-like blood-thinning compounds (a 2015 systematic review, Journal of Pharmacognosy and Phytochemistry), creating a real interaction risk with anticoagulant medication and blood-clotting disorders. This caution has been added directly to the monograph.
Curry leaf — blood sugar support (Monograph #136, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED): Multiple small human trials (e.g., Iyer & Mani 1990, Plant Foods for Human Nutrition, 30 patients) found real but modest and sometimes transient reductions in fasting/postprandial blood sugar with curry leaf supplementation, alongside a larger body of supportive animal research. This book’s “genuinely reasonable and growing body of research, including some human studies, supports modest… effects” framing is precisely accurate. No changes needed.
Scotch bonnet pepper — topical pain relief via capsaicin (Monograph #120, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, strongly): Capsaicin’s topical analgesic effect is among the most rigorously confirmed claims in this entire book: the FDA has approved an 8% capsaicin patch (Qutenza) specifically for post-herpetic neuralgia and diabetic peripheral neuropathy based on randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, and the TRPV1-receptor mechanism is well-characterized in the pharmacological literature. This book’s Tier 1 rating is fully earned. No changes needed.
Burdock root — skin/antioxidant &** blood sugar support (Monograph #12, Tier 2/3 — CONFIRMED):** Real search confirms mostly in vitro/animal-level evidence (ESCOP monograph, 2021; ScienceDirect ethnopharmacology review, 2022) with limited direct human trials for skin conditions specifically, and a documented ragweed-family (Asteraceae) allergy/anaphylaxis case report matching this book’s caution. This book’s conservative Tier 2/3 split (lab evidence promising, human trials limited) is accurate. No changes needed.
Mullein — respiratory/cough support (Monograph #24, Tier 3 — CONFIRMED): Real search confirms the European Medicines Agency’s herbal monograph for mullein flower is explicitly based on long-standing traditional use, not clinical trial evidence, and most laboratory support is test-tube level. This book’s Tier 3 (traditional use) framing, plus its distinctive and accurate caution about straining the leaf’s irritating fine hairs before drinking, is well-calibrated. No changes needed.
Okra — blood sugar support (Monograph #51, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED, evidence base is substantial): Multiple 2023–2026 systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (one pooling 14 RCTs across 836 participants) found statistically significant reductions in fasting blood glucose, HbA1c, and lipids with okra supplementation in type 2 diabetes and prediabetes patients — though the certainty of evidence is rated low to very low due to study-quality limitations across the field. This book’s “several human and animal studies suggest… modestly help, encouraging, not a treatment” framing is accurate and appropriately conservative given the quality caveats, even though the quantity of RCT evidence is more substantial than the modest framing might suggest. No changes needed.
Tamarind — digestive support (Monograph #43, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED, caution precisely matched): Real search confirms genuine laxative/digestive activity (fiber, tartaric acid, potassium content) and, notably, confirms this book’s specific caution word-for-word: tamarind has documented interactions that increase absorption/blood levels of aspirin and ibuprofen. This is an unusually precise match between the book’s caution and the primary literature. No changes needed.
Papaya (leaf and seed) — digestive enzyme &** antiparasitic use (Monograph #53, Tier 2/3 — CONFIRMED):** Real search confirms papain has genuine, multi-trial-supported topical wound-healing activity (several clinical trials totaling hundreds of patients, outperforming collagenase in some comparisons) and real digestive benefit in IBS-type symptoms. This book’s pregnancy caution (unripe fruit/concentrated leaf-seed preparations as a labor-inducing traditional use) is well-documented and accurately flagged. No changes needed.
Red palm oil — vitamin A/E content &** heart health (Monograph #68, Tier 1 for nutrients / “mixed/debated” for heart health — CONFIRMED, exceptionally well-calibrated):** Real search confirms vitamin A/beta-carotene bioavailability from red palm oil is genuinely excellent (Nutrition Reviews, 2017) — supporting the Tier 1 food-nutrient claim — while cholesterol/heart-health research is authentically mixed, with some studies showing improvement and others showing no change or worsening (AOCS review; Dr. Axe; Healthline). This book’s refusal to overstate a “heart-healthy” claim the field hasn’t settled is exactly the right call. No changes needed.
Sage — sore throat &** cognitive function (Monograph #23, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED, appropriately conservative):** This monograph does not claim a menopause/hot-flash benefit for sage, even though real search found this is actually sage’s best-supported human-trial claim (multiple double-blind, placebo-controlled RCTs, e.g. Bommer et al. 2011, Advances in Therapy; Dew Tober & Schoop 2021). The claims this book does make — sore throat gargle support and mild cognitive benefit (Kennedy/Tildesley studies on Salvia and cognition) — are independently real, and the thujone caution matches the wormwood-family concern accurately. No overclaim; no changes needed.
Yellow dock — iron-related tiredness (Monograph #38, Tier 3 — CONFIRMED): Real search confirms Drugs.com’s clinical assessment explicitly states no clinical data exists for any yellow dock use, matching this book’s honest “modern trials are lacking” framing. The oxalate caution is accurate and appropriately calibrated (present but manageable with normal preparation). No changes needed.
Coconut — hydration &** oil (Monograph #111 — CONFIRMED, with a real refinement made):** Coconut water’s Tier 1 rehydration claim is well-supported. For coconut oil, real search found current major health-authority consensus (AHA, British Heart Foundation, EUFIC, 2025–2026 sources) has moved past “genuinely contested” toward a fairly clear position that coconut oil raises LDL cholesterol similarly to other saturated fats, and that the popular MCT-based defense of coconut oil is a documented misconception — coconut oil’s dominant fatty acid (lauric acid) behaves like a long-chain saturated fat, not the true medium-chain triglycerides used in the supportive MCT research. The monograph’s “mixed/debated” framing has been tightened to reflect this more settled authority consensus while keeping the moderation-based caution unchanged.
Sesame seed (benne) — nutrition (Monograph #119, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, appropriately conservative): This monograph makes no cholesterol/blood-pressure claim at all, even though real search found decent RCT-based meta-analytic support exists for both (e.g., an 8-trial, 843-participant meta-analysis found significant systolic/diastolic BP reductions). The book sticks to the well-established calcium/nutrient Tier 1 claim and its Gullah Geechee linguistic-history framing, and its sesame-allergy caution is accurate and increasingly clinically relevant (sesame is now a recognized major allergen in US labeling law). No overclaim; no changes needed.
Marshmallow root — throat &** digestive soothing (Monograph #94, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED):** Real search confirms the mucilage-based soothing mechanism is endorsed by multiple European regulatory herbal bodies (German Commission E, WHO, ESCOP, EMA) based on long use and consumer-reported outcomes (one survey of 822 users), though controlled human trials remain limited — matching this book’s “well understood and plausible… direct rigorous human trials are limited” framing exactly. The medication-absorption-timing caution (shared with slippery elm) is a sound, accurate mechanistic point for mucilage herbs. No changes needed.
Watercress — nutrition &** antioxidant support (Monograph #60, Tier 1/2 — CONFIRMED, appropriately conservative):** This monograph does not claim a cancer-prevention benefit, even though real search found active early-stage human and preclinical research on this front (e.g., a 2025 narrative review of 88 sources; a small RCT in hemodialysis patients). The book’s more conservative Tier 1 nutrition / Tier 2 antioxidant framing avoids overclaiming an emerging research area. Its distinctive caution about wild-harvested watercress carrying waterborne parasites (liver fluke risk from contaminated water) is accurate and an important, often-overlooked real-world safety point. No changes needed.
Hydrangea root — kidney/urinary support (Monograph #27 — CONFIRMED, caution meaningfully strengthened): Real search confirms this plant carries a genuine and serious safety profile: all parts contain the cyanogenic glycoside hydrangin, and multiple clinical references (RxList, WebMD-style compilations) specify a concrete limit — no more than approximately 2 grams of dried root at a time, and not for extended periods. The original caution mentioned only vague “dizziness and gastrointestinal upset” without naming the mechanism or giving a concrete limit; this has been corrected to name the cyanogenic-glycoside mechanism explicitly and state the specific dose/duration guidance found in the literature.
Lemongrass (fever grass) — calm/sleep, digestive, antimicrobial (Monograph #7, Tier 3 — CONFIRMED, appropriately conservative): This monograph’s “human evidence is thin” framing for the calming-tea claim is borne out precisely: a double-blind clinical trial (Leite et al. 1986) testing lemongrass tea against placebo for anxiety in Brazil — where this traditional use is most established — found no significant difference from placebo. The book does not overclaim here. The essential-oil-not-for-internal-use caution is also correct; undiluted lemongrass oil has documented toxicity risk at high oral doses. No changes needed.
Bitter leaf — blood sugar &** antiparasitic use (Monograph #31, Tier 2/3 — CONFIRMED):** Real search confirms mostly animal/lab-level evidence for the blood-sugar claim (multiple rat studies) plus at least one small human clinical trial for a different traditional use (malaria, Challand & Willcox 2009, Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine). This book’s modest “encouraging but not a replacement for treatment” framing and diabetes-medication caution are accurate and appropriately calibrated. No changes needed.
Iboga — the strongest caution in the book (Monograph #108 — CONFIRMED, maximally rigorous already): Real search strongly confirms the severity of this monograph’s existing caution: peer-reviewed sources document at least 19-27 fatalities temporally associated with ibogaine ingestion, largely attributed to cardiac arrhythmias and long-QT syndrome (a case reported in the New England Journal of Medicine), with deaths occurring even in supervised clinical settings. No regulatory body has approved ibogaine for any use. This book’s existing framing — cultural inclusion without recommendation, explicit fatality risk named, no preparation guidance given — is already exactly right and needed no changes.
Wild yam — the “natural hormone” myth correction (Monograph #78 — CONFIRMED, precisely accurate): Real search confirms, in exact agreement with this book’s correction, that diosgenin (wild yam’s key compound) cannot be converted into progesterone, DHEA, or other hormones by the human body under any circumstance — that conversion requires a laboratory process (Marker degradation) discovered in the 1940s. A double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of wild yam cream for menopause symptoms found no significant difference from placebo. This book’s direct correction of one of the most persistent myths in the herbal marketplace is fully earned. No changes needed.
Black walnut hull — antiparasitic/antifungal use (Monograph #75 — CONFIRMED, with a real caution added): Real search confirms juglone’s genuine antimicrobial lab activity and confirms this book’s skin-irritant caution. An additional documented finding not in the original caution: liver toxicity has been reported specifically with concentrated black walnut hull extracts (as opposed to typical traditional-strength doses, which appear well tolerated short-term) — this caution has been added directly to the monograph.
Horsetail — diuretic &** hair/nail/connective tissue support (Monograph #72, Tier 2/3 — CONFIRMED):** Real search confirms the thiaminase caution is genuine and clinically documented (Drugs.com, RxList, a published case report of prenatal thiamine-deficiency exposure linked to horsetail use) — matching this book’s “standardized, reputable-source products rather than casual wild foraging” guidance precisely. No changes needed.
Rosemary — hair growth &** memory/alertness (Monograph #91, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED):** Real search confirms genuine human clinical trial support for both claims: topical rosemary oil has been tested against a standard hair-loss treatment with comparable results, and multiple RCTs (aromatherapy and oral) show measurable memory/mood benefits. This book’s Tier 2 framing and pregnancy/seizure-disorder cautions are accurate. No changes needed.
Holy basil (tulsi) — stress/cortisol &** blood sugar support (Monograph #92, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED, evidence base is strong):** Real search confirms multiple randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled human trials (e.g., a 100-participant 2022 trial, a 158-participant 2012 trial) showing significant reductions in perceived stress, cortisol, and improved sleep/cognitive measures. This is genuinely solid evidence — this book’s “growing body of human trials” framing is fair and, if anything, could be read as slightly conservative given the trial quality. No changes needed.
Slippery elm — throat &** digestive soothing (Monograph #73, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED):** Real search confirms slippery elm is FDA-OTC-recognized as a safe demulcent for sore throat, with LiverTox explicitly noting no evidence of liver injury risk. The medication-timing caution and even the elm-sustainability note match the real literature. No changes needed.
Buchu — urinary tract support (Monograph #121, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED, caution strengthened): Real search confirms mostly in vitro/animal-level evidence (a 2022 Frontiers review notes buchu became “largely obsolete” with the advent of antibiotics due to sparse modern efficacy evidence) matching this book’s “rigorous modern human trials are limited” framing. One real gap found: Drugs.com specifically documents uterine-stimulant effects for buchu, a more concrete finding than the original “limited safety data in pregnancy” phrasing conveyed — the caution has been strengthened to state avoidance in pregnancy directly rather than merely favoring caution.
Baobab leaf — nutrition (Monograph #148, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, well-scoped): This monograph correctly restricts its claim to the leaf specifically (calcium, iron, protein as a cooked vegetable) and does not import the fruit pulp’s separate evidence base (vitamin C, prebiotic fiber, a 2021 RCT on gut microbiota and a 2022 RCT on postprandial glycemia) — which the book appropriately covers in a separate baobab fruit entry elsewhere. This distinction-keeping between plant parts is accurate scientific practice. No changes needed.
Sassafras — the safrole carcinogen flag (Monograph #131 — CONFIRMED, already maximally accurate): Real search strongly confirms this monograph’s caution: safrole is FDA-banned as a food additive (since 1960), classified by the National Toxicology Program as “reasonably anticipated to be a human carcinogen,” and caused liver tumors in animal studies at multiple exposure routes. This book’s “does not recommend regular consumption… genuinely argues against casual home use” framing, with no preparation guidance given, is exactly right. No changes needed.
Pokeweed (poke salad) — the mandatory-preparation food safety flag (Monograph #132 — CONFIRMED, already maximally accurate): Real search confirms the double/triple-boiling preparation requirement is genuine and non-negotiable (multiple independent culinary and toxicology sources agree), that mature roots/leaves/berries are seriously toxic (lectins, phytolaccatoxin, alkaloids), and that child poisoning from berries is a documented real-world risk. This book’s “only prepare this dish if taught directly by someone experienced… never let children have unsupervised access” caution is exactly matched to the real danger. No changes needed.
Khat — cultural inclusion without recommendation (Monograph #140 — CONFIRMED, one real risk added): Real search confirms the documented cardiovascular (hypertension, cardiomyopathy), dependency, and legal-status findings. One specific and serious risk not explicitly named in the original text: published case reports document khat-induced psychotic disorder with heavy, prolonged use — this has been added by name rather than left folded into general “dependency-related concerns,” since psychosis is a distinct and serious psychiatric risk worth naming directly.
True yam — nutrition (Monograph #113, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED): This monograph already explicitly distinguishes true yam (Dioscorea rotundata/alata, a food crop) from wild yam (Dioscorea villosa, covered separately for its medicinal folk use and hormone-myth correction). Real search confirms true yam species are genuinely nutritious starch/fiber/mineral sources without the hormone-related claims that apply only to wild yam — the book’s species-level distinction-keeping is accurate and important. No changes needed.
Groundnut (peanut) — nutrition (Monograph #114, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, both cautions already present): Real search confirms both cautions this monograph already names — serious allergy risk and aflatoxin contamination risk (a genuine carcinogen concern especially relevant to improperly stored African-grown groundnuts, per multiple 2024-2025 food-safety reviews) — are the two real, documented risk categories for this food. No changes needed; already comprehensive.
Leaf of life (miracle leaf) — respiratory &** wound support (Monograph #127, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED, cardiac caution already precise):** Real search confirms the cardiac glycoside (bufadienolide) content is genuine and well-documented, including the veterinary literature on livestock cardiac poisoning from grazing that this monograph specifically references. The caution’s framing — real for concentrated/large doses, traditional modest tea use has a longer safety record, heart-condition awareness warranted — matches the clinical and toxicological literature closely. No changes needed.
Cassava root — the mandatory-processing food safety flag (Monograph #112 — CONFIRMED, already maximally accurate): Real search strongly confirms this monograph’s caution: improperly processed cassava remains a genuine, active public health concern, causing konzo (an irreversible paralytic neurological disease) in cassava-dependent communities today, particularly during drought/conflict when processing time is cut short. This book’s “tradition’s elaborate preparation steps exist purely because they are medically necessary” framing is exactly right. No changes needed.
Bitter kola — respiratory &** liver support (Monograph #107, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED):** Real search confirms mostly laboratory/animal-level evidence (kolaviron’s hepatoprotective and antimicrobial activity is well-studied at the preclinical level) with limited human trials, matching this book’s “human clinical trials remain more limited than the plant’s popularity would suggest” framing. The book’s distinction from true kola nut (a different genus, Cola vs. Garcinia) is also botanically accurate. No changes needed.
Mango leaf — blood sugar support (Monograph #117, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED): Real search confirms mostly animal-model evidence (multiple streptozotocin-induced diabetic rat studies) with only preliminary human data — a 2024 study explicitly states “subsequent human clinical trials would be crucial to confirm” the effects seen in animals. This book’s “some laboratory and preliminary human research… not established well enough to substitute for diabetes treatment” framing is accurately calibrated. No changes needed.
Guava fruit and guava leaf — nutrition and diarrhea support (Monographs #116 and #44 — CONFIRMED, both correctly separated): Real search confirms guava leaf has a genuinely reasonable evidence base for diarrhea, including a 2024 systematic review of human clinical trials with mostly positive results (though calling for further work to define clinical significance) — matching this book’s “genuinely reasonable body of studies, including some human trials” framing precisely, along with an appropriately firm “see a doctor for serious/prolonged diarrhea” safety net. The separate fruit entry correctly limits itself to a Tier 1 vitamin C/fiber nutrition claim without importing the leaf’s medicinal claims. No changes needed for either.
Pimento (allspice) — dental pain &** digestive support (Monograph #85, Tier 2/3 — CONFIRMED, appropriately conservative):** Real search confirms Drugs.com’s clinical assessment states plainly that “clinical studies are lacking” for allspice’s digestive applications — this book correctly keeps that claim at Tier 3 (traditional use) rather than citing an unverifiable “2018 double-blind trial” claim found circulating on a less rigorous source. The eugenol-based dental pain claim (Tier 2) is well-supported by the shared mechanism with clove, which this book already covers. No changes needed — this is good source discrimination.
Teff — nutrition (Monograph #138, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, one addition made): Real search confirms teff’s genuinely strong nutritional profile (iron, fiber, gluten-free, low glycemic index) across multiple 2025-2026 nutrition reviews. One documented but rare finding not in the original text: a published case report describes an allergic reaction to teff — a brief, appropriately scaled note has been added, consistent with how this book flags rare food allergies elsewhere (groundnut, sesame).
Spanish needles (Bidens pilosa) — anti-inflammatory activity (Monograph #130, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED): Real search confirms substantial preclinical/laboratory evidence across multiple countries, matching this book’s framing. Notably, this book does not make the antidiabetic claim that a genuine small human pilot study (2015, PMC) actually supports — while one lower-quality source circulated an apparently unverifiable “2020 double-blind RCT of 60 patients” claim that contradicts the more rigorous source’s own statement that no such trial had been conducted. The book’s caution about correct plant identification and clean sourcing for wild-foraged material is sound. No changes needed.
Fitweed (culantro) — digestive/anti-inflammatory use and the “fitweed” name (Monograph #128, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED, exemplary safety framing): Real search confirms mostly preclinical evidence for the digestive/anti-inflammatory claim, matching this book’s calibration. The direct, unambiguous flagging of the “fitweed” folk name’s seizure-treatment association as medically unsupported, with immediate redirection to emergency care, is exactly the right approach to a genuinely dangerous piece of folklore. No changes needed.
Society garlic — antimicrobial activity (Monograph #149, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED): Real search confirms mostly laboratory-level antimicrobial evidence (a 2016 Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine review notes “little scientific research has been conducted to validate its use” beyond preclinical studies), matching this book’s “reasonable laboratory evidence… direct human clinical trials are limited” framing. No changes needed.
Passion fruit — nutrition (Monograph #146, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, appropriately scoped): This monograph correctly limits its claim to fresh fruit nutrition (vitamin C, fiber, antioxidants) and does not import passionflower’s separate calming reputation, which the book already covers as a distinct leaf/flower entry. A specialized peel-flour diabetes trial exists in the literature but concerns a different, more processed product than the fresh fruit this monograph describes — its absence is a reasonable scope decision, not a gap. No changes needed.
Marula — nutrition &** skin use (Monograph #123, Tier 1/2 — CONFIRMED):** Real search strongly confirms marula fruit’s exceptionally high vitamin C content (multiple studies report 62–403 mg/100g, several times that of orange juice), matching this book’s “among the highest of any commonly eaten fruit” claim precisely. The kernel oil’s skin-moisturizing evidence is also independently supported. No changes needed.
Kigelia (sausage tree) — skin use (Monograph #124 — CONFIRMED, caution strengthened): Real search confirms this book’s discretion in NOT making an unproven “treats skin cancer” claim — a real folk reputation that only isolated cell-line/lab studies partially support, with no human trials. A specific, serious, and previously under-named risk was found and added directly: raw, unprocessed kigelia fruit has been documented (USDA) to cause severe vomiting and liver damage if eaten — the caution previously said only “not intended for eating” without explaining why; it now names the actual danger.
Waterleaf — nutrition (Monograph #125, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, appropriately conservative): Real search confirms waterleaf’s genuine iron/vitamin A/C/antioxidant density, and confirms the book correctly avoids importing the plant’s separate cognitive-function, antidiabetic, and anti-inflammatory research, which remains entirely at the animal/preclinical stage. The oxalate caution is standard and accurate for a leafy green. No changes needed.
Ewedu (jute leaf) — nutrition &** digestive comfort (Monograph #126, Tier 1/3 — CONFIRMED, appropriately conservative):** Real search confirms the mucilage-based digestive comfort mechanism (Tier 3) and rich nutrient profile (Tier 1) match the evidence, while the book correctly avoids the plant’s separate anti-inflammatory/antidiabetic claims, which remain rodent-model only. One preliminary rat study found a dose-dependent uterine-muscle-relaxant effect from concentrated extract — too thin and preclinical a finding to warrant a caution change for normal culinary soup consumption. No changes needed.
Utazi — blood sugar &** digestive support (Monograph #150 — CONFIRMED, two real corrections made):** Real search found an actual human trial (Ugochukwu & Babady, adult Nigerian subjects) showing hypoglycemic and hypolipidemic effects — the original text’s “human clinical trials remain limited” undersold this; the wording has been corrected to note this single, older human study exists rather than implying none does. More importantly, multiple independent sources document a genuine uterine-stimulant/miscarriage risk from utazi — the original caution addressed only postpartum timing, not the separate and more serious risk of use during pregnancy itself. Both corrections have been made directly in the monograph.
Yellowroot — antimicrobial/astringent use (Monograph #134 — CONFIRMED, one real caution added): Real search confirms the berberine-family mechanism and existing pregnancy caution are accurate (Drugs.com confirms berberine crosses the placenta and is linked to neonatal jaundice/kernicterus). One additional documented finding not previously included: a published case report (Parsons, 1981, North Carolina Medical Journal) links chronic arsenic poisoning to a contaminated yellowroot tea product — a real sourcing/quality caution that has been added directly to the monograph.
Life everlasting (rabbit tobacco) — respiratory support (Monograph #135, Tier 3 — CONFIRMED, already well-calibrated): Real search confirms the traditional smoking method for asthma/respiratory complaints is genuine folk practice, but also confirms modern sources uniformly advise against inhaling smoke of any kind, especially for anyone with asthma or COPD. This book’s choice to recommend tea preparation instead of smoking, while keeping the claim itself at Tier 3 (traditional use, essentially no rigorous human trials), is exactly the right calibration. No changes needed.
Bitter bush (Chromolaena odorata) — topical wound healing (Monograph #129 — CONFIRMED, one real caution added): Real search confirms genuine laboratory support for the topical wound-healing/hemostatic claim (multiple studies on fibroblast proliferation and clotting-related gene expression). A real and separate finding not previously addressed: the plant contains pyrrolizidine-alkaloid-family compounds, and toxicology studies found liver damage at higher internal/oral doses, with one review explicitly stating oral administration is not advised. Since this book’s traditional-use description covers topical first aid only, an explicit caution against oral/internal preparations of this plant has been added to prevent a reader from assuming topical safety extends to tea or other internal use.
Uziza (West African pepper) — digestive &** anti-inflammatory activity (Monograph #80, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED):** Real search confirms genuine laboratory/animal-level anti-inflammatory and analgesic activity (multiple rat studies, including comparisons to diclofenac/aspirin), with no human clinical trials identified — matching this book’s “reasonable laboratory evidence… human clinical trials are limited” precisely. No changes needed.
Grains of paradise — digestive &** metabolic support (Monograph #18, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED):** Real search confirms genuine small human clinical trials exist (2013/2015 Japanese randomized, placebo-controlled crossover studies showing increased energy expenditure and reduced visceral fat via brown-adipose-tissue activation) — matching this book’s “human clinical trials are limited but growing” framing exactly. No changes needed.
African basil (efirin) — antimicrobial &** digestive support (Monograph #19 — CONFIRMED, pregnancy caution strengthened):** Real search confirms good laboratory antimicrobial evidence with no human clinical trials (Drugs.com: “clinical data are lacking to support use for any indication”). One specific, documented finding not previously named: Drugs.com and related literature specifically flag reported abortifacient effects for this plant — the original “limited safety data in pregnancy” phrasing has been strengthened to name this specific, more serious risk directly.
Man piaba (Eclipta/bhringraj) — hair health &** liver support (Monograph #142 — CONFIRMED, real corrections made):** Real search found an actual 24-week human clinical trial (54 participants) showing meaningful hair-shedding improvement with standardized Eclipta extract — the original “rigorous large-scale human trials are limited” phrasing undersold this; corrected to note genuine human data exists as a single trial. Real search also found this plant’s traditional cholagogue (bile-stimulating) action carries a documented caution around gallstones and blood-thinning medication that wasn’t previously named — added directly to the monograph.
Aidan fruit — blood pressure &** metabolic support (Monograph #110, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED, appropriately conservative):** Real search confirms mostly animal/rat-level evidence for blood pressure and metabolic claims, matching this book’s calibration. Notably, this monograph correctly avoids the sensationalized “epilepsy treatment” framing that circulated in some press coverage (e.g., Newsweek) — that anticonvulsant finding is animal-study-only and this book doesn’t import it as a human-relevant claim. No changes needed.
Yohimbe — erectile function, with serious cautions (Monograph #46 — CONFIRMED, one life-threatening gap closed): Real search strongly confirms this book’s already-thorough caution: NCCIH, LiverTox, and multiple case-report compilations confirm cardiac arrhythmia, heart attacks, seizures, and hypertensive crisis risk, plus FDA classification as an unsafe herb and restriction/banning in multiple countries. One specific and life-threatening gap found: the documented MAOI-antidepressant interaction (potentially dangerous) and SSRI/serotonin-syndrome-type risk were not previously named specifically — this has been added directly to the monograph’s caution.
Chaparral — the strongest caution in the book (Monograph #37 — CONFIRMED, already maximally accurate): Real search strongly confirms this monograph’s framing: LiverTox and Memorial Sloan Kettering both confirm chaparral has caused severe hepatotoxicity including cases requiring liver transplantation, and no rigorous human clinical evidence supports its cancer, arthritis, or detox marketing claims. This book’s absolute “does not recommend chaparral for internal use under any circumstance” stance is exactly matched to the severity of the real evidence. No changes needed.
Ackee — the mandatory-ripeness food safety flag (Monograph #63 — CONFIRMED, one precise clarification added): Real search strongly confirms this book’s caution, including the specific real finding that StatPearls/NCBI explicitly state: cooking does NOT neutralize hypoglycin toxicity in unripe fruit — ripeness is the safety factor, not cooking. The original text’s “must be well cooked” phrasing could be read as implying cooking is a safeguard against unripe fruit; this has been clarified directly, along with a warning against reusing cooking water from unripe ackee (a documented risk factor).
Kanna — mood/stress support (Monograph #48 — CONFIRMED, already precisely calibrated): Real search confirms the SSRI/MAOI serotonin-syndrome interaction risk this book already flags is the single most important safety consideration for this plant, and confirms genuine small human RCTs exist (Chiu et al. 2014, standardized Zembrin extract) — matching this book’s “modern standardized extracts now studied more rigorously than most plants in this book” framing exactly. No changes needed.
Hoodia — appetite suppression, unproven (Monograph #49 — CONFIRMED, already precisely calibrated): Real search confirms Drugs.com’s statement that peer-reviewed RCTs evaluating hoodia’s efficacy are lacking, and that a real 15-day RCT (Blom 2011) found no meaningful weight-loss benefit over placebo with notable GI side effects. This book’s “unproven” tier, quality-control warning, and Indigenous-knowledge-exploitation framing are all accurately calibrated. No changes needed.
Black seed — blood sugar &** blood pressure support (Monograph #41, Tier 2 edging toward Tier 1 — CONFIRMED, strongly):** Real search confirms this is genuinely one of the most heavily-trialed plants in the book — an 82-RCT dose-response meta-analysis (2025) and multiple other systematic reviews confirm significant reductions in blood glucose, lipids, and blood pressure. This book’s “edging toward Tier 1” framing is well-earned and, if anything, could be read as still slightly conservative. No changes needed.
Avocado leaf — traditional digestive/menstrual use (Monograph #56, Tier 3 — CONFIRMED, well-calibrated): Real search confirms persin (the compound responsible for well-documented cardiotoxicity in animals, especially birds and livestock) does not translate to meaningful human risk at normal doses according to rigorous toxicology sources — this book correctly avoids raising an animal-specific fear that wouldn’t apply to humans, while still flagging the traditional, real caution around uterine/menstrual effects. No changes needed.
African mango — weight/metabolic markers (Monograph #47, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED, appropriately skeptical): Real search found genuine RCTs (three trials, ~214 total participants) reporting large weight-loss effects, but also found that a rigorous DARE-quality-assessed systematic review concluded Irvingia could not yet be recommended as a weight-loss aid pending better-quality, more independent trials — largely because the existing trials come from an overlapping small research group. This book’s “evidence base is thinner and more mixed than the marketing… treat aggressive marketing with real skepticism” framing correctly weighs the independent skepticism over the large headline numbers in the primary studies. No changes needed.
Honey — wound care &** cough (Monograph #34B — CONFIRMED, one real nuance added):** Real search confirms strong evidence for acute wounds and burns (multiple RCTs, e.g., 32% complete healing at 6 weeks vs. 0% for povidone iodine in one trial) and for cough. One real nuance found: a large RCT (Jull et al., 187 venous leg ulcer patients) found no significant benefit over usual care for chronic wounds specifically, and the German Society for Wound Healing explicitly does not recommend honey for chronic wound treatment. The monograph’s Tier 1 wound-care claim has been refined to specify it applies to acute wounds and burns, where the evidence is genuinely strong, rather than chronic wounds, where it is weaker.
True cinnamon vs. cassia — blood sugar &** the coumarin distinction (Monograph #61 — CONFIRMED, already precisely calibrated):** Real search strongly confirms the coumarin/liver-toxicity distinction between Ceylon and cassia cinnamon (cassia can carry roughly 100–250x the coumarin of Ceylon, with documented case reports of liver enzyme elevation from heavy cassia use) and the real blood-sugar benefit shown in multiple human trials. No changes needed.
Sour orange/bitter orange leaf — calm &** sleep (Monograph #55, Tier 3 — CONFIRMED, already precisely calibrated):** Real search on bitter orange (Citrus aurantium) synephrine/cardiovascular research applies specifically to peel/fruit extracts used in weight-loss products — a genuinely contested area with mixed meta-analytic findings and industry-funded reviews on one side. This monograph correctly and explicitly separates the traditional calming leaf tea (which it endorses cautiously) from the peel/fruit synephrine extracts (which it explicitly does not endorse) — exactly the right plant-part distinction. No changes needed.
Broadleaf plantain (plantain weed) — topical wound/skin soothing (Monograph #50 — CONFIRMED, tier upgraded with real new evidence): Real search found genuine, recent human clinical trials that didn’t exist when “formal human clinical trials are limited” was likely written — a randomized controlled trial on diabetic foot and pressure ulcers, and a case-control study finding Plantago major ointment comparable to standard silver sulfadiazine treatment for second-degree burns. The claim has been upgraded from Tier 3 to Tier 2 to reflect this genuine, if still limited, human evidence base.
Locust bean (dawadawa/iru) — nutrition &** fermented-food gut support (Monograph #66, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED):** Real search confirms strong microbiological evidence (multiple 2025 studies confirming probiotic bacterial strains like Lactobacillus and Bacillus with real gastric-acid and bile-salt tolerance) and rich nutritional composition (35-40% protein), but no human clinical health-outcome trials specific to dawadawa — matching this book’s “plausibly supportive… specific clinical trials on dawadawa itself are limited” framing precisely. No changes needed.
Prodigiosa (women’s tongue/goat bush) — blood sugar support (Monograph #36, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED): Real search on the Brickellia genus (this monograph covers B. cavanillesii specifically, closely related to the more commonly documented B. grandiflora) confirms mostly animal/lab-level evidence for the blood-sugar claim, a real documented uterine-stimulant/pregnancy concern, and a real diabetes-medication interaction risk (additive hypoglycemia) — all matching this book’s “some laboratory and preliminary studies… avoid in pregnancy… involve their doctor” framing. No changes needed.
Shea — skin moisturizing &** minor wound support (Monograph #42, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED):** Real search confirms genuine supportive evidence, including RCT data (a French moisturizer study and a 2022 atopic dermatitis trial including shea butter as a formulation component) showing real anti-inflammatory and moisturizing benefit. This book’s “good evidence… commonly used in modern dermatology-adjacent products” framing and tree-nut-allergy caution are both accurate. No changes needed.
Cayenne pepper — topical pain relief &** metabolism (Monograph #62 — CONFIRMED, one real caution added):** Real search confirms the Tier 1 topical pain-relief claim (same FDA-approved-drug-level evidence as scotch bonnet’s capsaicin) and real human trial support for metabolic/thermogenic effects (calorie-burning and appetite studies). One real, documented finding not previously included: cayenne has genuine mild blood-thinning activity, creating a real interaction concern for anyone on blood-thinning or blood-pressure medication taking concentrated supplements — this has been added directly to the monograph.
Cassava leaf — nutrition, with a serious processing caution (Monograph #64 — CONFIRMED, already maximally appropriate): Real search confirms — and if anything strengthens — this book’s serious framing: cassava leaves actually contain higher cyanogenic glycoside concentrations than the root itself (roughly 5g linamarin/kg fresh weight in leaves versus 10-20x lower in roots per toxicology literature), making the “genuine and serious safety flag” language fully earned rather than overstated. No changes needed.
Callaloo (amaranth greens) — nutrition (Monograph #70, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED): Real search confirms a genuinely rich nutrient profile and confirms the more rigorous peer-reviewed literature groups amaranth with spinach as a high-oxalate green (5,138-12,576 mg/100g dry matter range), directly contradicting a less rigorous marketing claim found elsewhere that amaranth is “lower oxalate than spinach.” This book’s oxalate/kidney-stone caution correctly sides with the more rigorous science. No changes needed.
Breadfruit — nutrition &** blood sugar (Monograph #69, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED):** Real search confirms genuine, if small-scale, supportive evidence (glycemic index research placing breadfruit favorably compared to white rice/potato, plus small feeding studies in diabetic patients). This book’s “some preliminary research… a matter of portion, not avoidance” framing appropriately avoids overclaiming these small studies as robust clinical proof. The honest historical framing of breadfruit’s plantation-economics origin is also accurate. No changes needed.
Cloves — dental/tooth pain (Monograph #45 — CONFIRMED, two real gaps closed): Real search strongly confirms the Tier 1 dental claim (multiple RCTs, including a pediatric injection-site trial where clove oil outperformed lidocaine gel and ice for pain/anxiety) and confirms two real, documented risks not previously specific enough: children ingesting clove oil have suffered seizures and serious liver damage requiring hospitalization (not just “burns,” which the caution said), and clove oil has documented mild blood-thinning activity creating a real anticoagulant interaction risk. Both have been added directly to the monograph.
Annatto (achiote) — antioxidant content (Monograph #54, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED): Real search confirms mostly animal/lab-level antioxidant evidence, with the annatto seed pigment (bixin) widely used and generally recognized as safe as a food color, and no major documented interactions at culinary/food levels — matching this book’s conservative, non-overclaiming framing. No changes needed.
