Honeybush — antioxidant activity &** menopausal comfort (Monograph #32 — CONFIRMED):** Real search confirms genuine phytoestrogenic and antioxidant compounds (mangiferin, hesperidin) with mostly preclinical/animal-level evidence — matching this book’s “human trials still developing… clinical evidence is preliminary” framing precisely for both claims. No changes needed.
Egusi seed — nutrition (Monograph #106, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED): Real search confirms genuinely high protein (23-37%) and fat (45-50%) content across multiple compositional analyses, matching this book’s “genuinely rich in protein and healthy fats” framing exactly. No changes needed.
Taro/cocoyam leaf — nutrition, with a serious cooking caution (Monograph #88 — CONFIRMED, one real nuance corrected): Real search confirms the raw-taro raphide toxicity caution is accurate and serious (documented cases including renal complications). One real nuance found: the original “traditional lengthy cooking methods fully neutralize this” overstated the case — cooking neutralizes the acute raphide-irritation danger, but taro remains a genuinely higher-oxalate food even when properly cooked (soaking alone does not remove it), and dedicated food-safety sources specifically advise kidney-stone-prone individuals to still moderate intake. This has been corrected directly in the monograph.
Sugarcane — nutrition, with honest historical framing (Monograph #101, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED): Real search confirms this book correctly avoids importing preliminary cell-based antioxidant/diabetes research (Caco-2 cell studies, not human trials) as a health claim, sticking instead to the modest, accurate claim that minimally processed cane retains some minerals lost in refining. No changes needed.
Plantain (the food) — nutrition &** digestive comfort (Monograph #102, Tier 1/3 — CONFIRMED, appropriately conservative):** Real search confirms this book correctly avoids importing plantain’s separate resistant-starch/diabetes-management research (mostly rat-model studies, with human data limited to a 10-participant glycemic-index study) as a treatment claim, sticking to solid Tier 1 nutrition and Tier 3 traditional digestive comfort. No changes needed.
Sorghum — nutrition (Monograph #103, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED): Real search confirms genuine gluten-free safety (confirmed by genome analysis for celiac patients) and antioxidant content that varies meaningfully by variety — this book’s “particularly in darker-colored varieties” nuance precisely matches real findings that brown sorghum specifically shows the highest antioxidant activity and lowest glycemic index among tested genotypes. No changes needed.
Millet — nutrition &** blood sugar, with a real thyroid nuance (Monograph #104 — CONFIRMED, already precisely calibrated):** Real search strongly confirms this book’s thyroid caution: pearl millet specifically contains C-glycosylflavones with documented TPO-inhibiting (goitrogenic) activity (a seminal 1989 JCEM study), though the effect is dose-dependent and mainly relevant to heavy consumers, existing thyroid conditions, or iodine-deficient populations — exactly matching this book’s “minor point worth a doctor’s awareness for heavy consumers, not a reason for ordinary dietary avoidance” framing. No changes needed.
Cowpea (black-eyed pea) — nutrition (Monograph #115, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED): Real search confirms genuinely excellent protein/fiber/folate content, plus a real human RCT (38 adults) showing cowpea protein reduced LDL cholesterol by 18.9% compared to casein over six weeks — the book’s conservative Tier 1 nutrition framing (not importing the still-preliminary diabetes/anti-inflammatory claims) is appropriately calibrated. No changes needed.
Fonio — nutrition (Monograph #105, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED): Real search confirms fonio’s distinctive amino acid profile — genuinely rich in methionine and cysteine, sulfur-containing amino acids uncommon in most grains — matching this book’s “good source of amino acids relative to many other grains” precisely. No changes needed.
African nutmeg (calabash nutmeg) — digestive &** postpartum use (Monograph #109, Tier 3 — CONFIRMED):** Real search confirms this book’s botanical distinction is accurate — Monodora myristica belongs to an entirely different plant family (Annonaceae) than true nutmeg (Myristicaceae, Myristica fragrans), meaning it doesn’t carry true nutmeg’s well-known myristicin-toxicity profile at high doses. Real search also confirms mostly animal/lab-level evidence for the traditional claims, matching the Tier 3 framing. No changes needed.
Genip — nutrition, with a real choking-hazard caution already present (Monograph #89 — CONFIRMED): Real search confirms genuine vitamin C/antioxidant content matching this book’s modest Tier 2 nutrition claim, and the monograph’s choking-hazard caution (large, smooth central seed, especially risky for young children) already reflects the real, documented safety concern associated with how this fruit is traditionally eaten. No changes needed.
Niger seed — nutrition (Monograph #147, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED, appropriately conservative): Real search confirms genuinely high unsaturated fat and antioxidant content, while this book correctly avoids importing the more preliminary antidiabetic/cardioprotective claims (mostly preclinical) as anything beyond general nutrition. No changes needed.
Wild lettuce — sleep &** mild pain (Monograph #71 — CONFIRMED, real factual correction made):** Real search across multiple rigorous sources (Drugs.com, Healthline, ScienceInsights) confirms a meaningful factual error in the original text: wild lettuce contains no actual opioid compounds and does not act on opioid pathways — the “lettuce opium” nickname is genuinely misleading, and its sedative/analgesic compounds (lactucin and related sesquiterpene lactones) work through an entirely different, less-understood mechanism. This has been corrected directly, similar in spirit to this book’s earlier wild yam hormone-myth correction, while preserving the real cautions around sedative-medication interaction, pregnancy, and glaucoma.
Baobab fruit — nutrition &** blood sugar support (Monograph #30, Tier 1/2 — CONFIRMED):** Real search strongly confirms baobab fruit pulp’s exceptional vitamin C content (200+ mg/100g, roughly 5-10x oranges) and confirms real human trials showing modestly reduced postprandial blood glucose response — matching this book’s “well-documented… encouraging, not conclusive” framing precisely for both claims. No changes needed.
Christmas bush (Jamaican) — traditional use (Monograph #143, Tier 3 — CONFIRMED, appropriately hedged already): Real search confirms “Christmas bush” is a genuinely confused common name in the botanical literature — most published research (anti-inflammatory, sickle cell studies) concerns the West/Central African species Alchornea cordifolia rather than the Jamaican Alchornea latifolia this monograph specifically names. This book’s explicit acknowledgment of regional naming ambiguity and its conservative “correct identification from a knowledgeable local source” caution is exactly the right response to this genuine identification problem. No changes needed.
Golden apple (ambarella) — nutrition (Monograph #90, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED): Real search confirms genuine, moderate vitamin C content (roughly 20-42 mg/100g across studies) — this book’s modest “genuinely good source of vitamin C” framing correctly avoids an inflated marketing claim found elsewhere (“30 times more vitamin C than oranges”), which the more rigorous compositional literature does not support. No changes needed.
Grains of Selim (negro pepper) — digestive &** antimicrobial use (Monograph #35 — CONFIRMED, one real gap closed):** Real search confirms genuine laboratory antimicrobial evidence matching this book’s Tier 2 framing. One real, separate finding not previously addressed: this plant has documented traditional use as a contraceptive in some West African communities, and animal studies have found reproductive-organ effects at concentrated doses — this is distinct from the postpartum-dosing caution already present and has been added directly, advising avoidance of concentrated use during pregnancy or when trying to conceive.
Camwood — topical skin use (Monograph #79, Tier 3 — CONFIRMED): Real search confirms mostly animal/lab-level evidence for antimicrobial and antioxidant activity, with no rigorous human clinical trials, matching this book’s conservative Tier 3 framing. The infant-skin patch-test caution is sensible given the plant’s real traditional use in newborn skin care. No changes needed.
Bay rum tree — topical muscle relief (Monograph #86 — CONFIRMED, one real caution added): Real search confirms genuine toxicity if ingested (matching this book’s “not intended for internal consumption”) and confirms this oil is high in eugenol, the same compound found in clove — which carries documented mild blood-thinning activity. This anticoagulant-interaction caution has been added directly, consistent with how this book already handles clove and cayenne’s similar eugenol/capsaicin-related findings.
Star apple leaf — blood sugar support (Monograph #87, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED, one real caution added): Real search confirms mostly animal/lab-level evidence for the blood-sugar claim, matching this book’s calibration. One documented finding not previously included: an animal study found the leaf extract toxic and lethal at very high concentrated doses (>30g/L) — distinct from the modest amounts used in ordinary tea, and worth naming as a reason to avoid concentrated extracts specifically. Added directly to the monograph.
Periwinkle — the plant-to-pharmaceutical story (Monograph #83 — CONFIRMED, already exceptional): Real search strongly confirms every element of this entry: vincristine and vinblastine are indeed real, FDA-approved chemotherapy drugs derived from Madagascar periwinkle that transformed survival rates for childhood leukemia and Hodgkin’s lymphoma, discovered via traditional diabetes-remedy research in the 1950s-60s. This book’s clear separation between the pharmaceutical derivatives (Tier 1) and the raw plant (a direct caution against home use) is precisely and powerfully accurate. No changes needed — one of the best-calibrated entries in the book.
Enset (false banana) — nutrition &** food security (Monograph #139 — CONFIRMED, one real nuance added):** Real search confirms enset’s genuine food-security value (staple for over 20 million Ethiopians, resilient to drought) matching this book’s “caloric staple” framing. One real nutritional nuance found and added: published research on enset-dependent communities specifically documents the crop as calorie-dense but relatively poor in protein and micronutrients, recommending dietary diversification alongside it — distinct from claiming complete nutritional value. Added directly to the monograph.
Naseberry (sapodilla) — nutrition (Monograph #141, Tier 1 — CONFIRMED): Real search confirms genuine fiber, vitamin C, iron, and tannin-based antioxidant content, with the book appropriately avoiding the still-preclinical antimicrobial/anti-inflammatory research. The unripe-fruit astringency caution matches the plant’s real saponin/tannin profile. No changes needed.
Otaheite apple (mountain apple) — nutrition (Monograph #144, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED): Real search confirms genuine vitamin C and antioxidant content (phenolics, anthocyanins) with mostly preclinical antiglycemic research that this book appropriately does not import as a claim. No changes needed.
Sea grape — nutrition (Monograph #145, Tier 2 — CONFIRMED, correct species specified): Real search reveals a genuine naming confusion in this space — “sea grape” also refers to an unrelated Asia-Pacific seaweed (Caulerpa) with much more extensive (and irrelevant) metabolic research. This monograph correctly specifies Coccoloba uvifera by botanical name and keeps its claim appropriately modest (general antioxidant content, not extensive medicinal research), correctly avoiding any conflation with the unrelated seaweed’s research base. No changes needed.
*Citation Batches 1–52 — RESULT FOR THE ORIGINAL 150: All 150 monographs verified. 146 original tier ratings/cautions confirmed accurate; twenty-six of those gained corrected/strengthened/refined cautions from real search; three (cascara sagrada, feverfew, valerian) corrected and downgraded from their original tier. This concluded the retroactive citation-verification pass on the manuscript’s first 150 monographs — see the note below on how monographs 151–200 were sourced.
SOURCING NOTE AND BIBLIOGRAPHY: MONOGRAPHS 151–200

exact_claim_text: Kenaf leaf: Young leaves cooked as a vegetable or brewed into tea; seeds pressed for oil or used in food applications.
complete_source_block: Preparation. Young leaves cooked as a vegetable or brewed into tea; seeds pressed for oil or used in food applications.
